items.title: Newton's method finds square roots in just a few steps
items.claim: To estimate sqrt(2): guess 1.5. Improve by averaging 1.5 with 2/1.5 = 1.333. New estimate: 1.417. Repeat with 2/1.417 = 1.412. New: 1.414. Already 4 decimals of accuracy in 2 steps from a poor start.
items.prompt: Why does this rapid convergence happen?

options.text: Newton's method converges QUADRATICALLY near a simple root: each step roughly DOUBLES the number of correct digits. 4 iterations of 10 correct digits each gives 16 digits — far faster than linear convergence
It is the only method that works on square roots
All iterative methods converge equally fast

items.reveal:
Newton-Raphson iteration: to solve f(x) = 0, iterate x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n). Geometrically: draw tangent at current point, take where it crosses the x-axis as next estimate.

For sqrt(a), solve f(x) = x^2 - a = 0. f'(x) = 2x. Iteration: x_(n+1) = x_n - (x_n^2 - a)/(2x_n) = (x_n + a/x_n)/2. This is the 'Babylonian method' — known since ~1700 BC.

Convergence rate: if x_n is the current estimate and r is the true root, |x_(n+1) - r| is roughly proportional to |x_n - r|^2. The error squares at each step — quadratic convergence. Roughly: number of correct digits doubles per iteration.

Starting from 1.5 for sqrt(2) (true value 1.41421...):
Step 1: 1.41667 (3 correct digits)
Step 2: 1.41421568 (6 correct digits)
Step 3: 1.414213562373... (12+ correct digits)
Step 4: limited only by floating-point precision.

Newton's method can also fail:
- If f'(x) = 0 nearby, division by zero or huge steps.
- For multi-root or degenerate roots, convergence is only linear.
- Bad initial guesses can cycle, diverge, or jump to a different root.

Fractal basins of attraction: for complex polynomial roots, Newton's method partitions the plane into 'basins' that have fractal boundaries. The Newton fractal is one of the prettiest objects in computational mathematics.
items.why: Iterative methods for solving equations look like trial and error. Newton-Raphson is far better — each step squares the precision, making it the workhorse of computational mathematics.

items.title: A note in a margin that took 358 years to verify
items.claim: Pierre de Fermat wrote in 1637 that he had a proof — too long for the margin — that a to the n + b to the n equals c to the n has no positive-integer solutions for n greater than 2. Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.
items.prompt: Why was Fermat's Last Theorem so hard to prove?

options.text: Fermat lied about having a proof — there isn't one

It was eventually shown to be equivalent to a statement about modular forms and elliptic curves (the Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture); the modern proof required machinery that didn't exist until the 1980s
Number theorists weren't trying hard enough
It is undecidable in standard axioms

items.reveal_title: Wiles, Frey, Ribet — a chain of insights
items.reveal:
Fermat wrote his marginal note in Diophantus's Arithmetica. Hundreds of mathematicians attempted the proof. Special cases were handled (n = 4 by Fermat himself; n = 3 by Euler; n = 5, 7 in the 1800s).

In 1985, Frey proposed that any non-trivial solution would correspond to an unusual elliptic curve. In 1986, Ribet proved this curve could not be 'modular'. Combined with the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture (all elliptic curves are modular), no solution could exist.

Wiles worked in secret for seven years on Taniyama-Shimura for a key class of elliptic curves. He announced the proof in 1993. A gap was found. With Richard Taylor he repaired it in late 1994. The proof runs over 100 pages and uses 20th-century algebraic geometry that Fermat couldn't have had.

It's almost certain Fermat did not have a real proof. He probably had a flawed attempt for small cases, since he never mentioned the result in subsequent letters.
items.why: Fermat's Last Theorem feels like an elementary statement about integers. Its proof needed centuries of machinery — number theory, algebraic geometry, automorphic forms — that no one in 1637 could have imagined.

items.title: The cubic formula forced mathematicians to take imaginary numbers seriously
items.claim: Cardano's 1545 formula for cubic equations works perfectly — but its intermediate steps require taking square roots of negative numbers, even when the final answer is a real number. The formula computes real answers via imaginary intermediates.
items.prompt: Why do imaginaries appear in real-answer cubics?

options.text: For cubics with three real roots, Cardano's formula expresses each root as a sum of two cube roots that individually are complex numbers; the imaginary parts cancel in the sum, but cannot be avoided algebraically — this is the 'casus irreducibilis'
Imaginary numbers can be avoided with smarter algebra
Cubics with real roots are computed without complex numbers

items.reveal_title: Casus irreducibilis and the unavoidability of complex numbers
items.reveal:
Cardano's formula for x^3 + px + q = 0:
x = cube root of (-q/2 + sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)) + cube root of (-q/2 - sqrt(q^2/4 + p^3/27)).

When all three roots are real, q^2/4 + p^3/27 is NEGATIVE — so you must take square roots of negatives. The cube roots are complex; their sum is real.

Example: x^3 - 15x - 4 = 0 has solutions x = 4, x = -2 plus or minus sqrt(3). All real.

Cardano's formula gives:
x = cube root of (2 + 11i) + cube root of (2 - 11i)

It's verifiable that 2 + 11i = (2 + i)^3 and 2 - 11i = (2 - i)^3. So x = (2 + i) + (2 - i) = 4. Real answer, computed through imaginary intermediates.

This is called casus irreducibilis (Cardano's term). For three real roots, there is no trigonometric-free, complex-number-free formula. The need for complex numbers is essential, not an avoidable trick.

This forced 16th-17th century mathematicians to take the 'sophistic quantities' seriously. The cubic was the gateway that pushed complex numbers from curiosity into necessity. They would only become geometrically intuitive with Wessel/Argand/Gauss in the 1790s-1830s — but their usefulness was inescapable from 1545 onward.

The quartic was solved by Cardano's student Ferrari (also published in Ars Magna). The quintic, as Galois and Abel showed centuries later, cannot be solved by radicals at all.
items.why: Real-world problems suggest only real numbers. The algebra of cubics shows that even the simplest real-coefficient real-root polynomials force complex arithmetic in their solution. Imaginaries aren't optional.
